 I. INTRODUCTION

This is the Third Progress Report to the Board of Executive Directors (the Board) on the
implementation of the Management Action Plan (MAP) in response to the Inspection Panel
Investigation Report No. (INSP/144751-IN) on the India – Rural Water Supply and Sanitation
Project for Low Income States (P132173) (the Project).
1.

The Project. The Project was a US$1.0 billion operation, of which the International
Development Association (IDA) financed US$500 million equivalent, and the rest was funded by
the Government of India (34 percent), the governments of the Project states (16 percent) and
beneficiary contributions (0.1 percent). The Project was approved on December 30, 2013, with a
planned duration of six years. Implemented in the states of Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand and Uttar
Pradesh, the Project supported investments to improve water supply and sanitation, including
construction of new infrastructure and rehabilitation and expansion of existing schemes.
2.

The Project was restructured in 2019. This included: (i) cancellation of US$250 million of
the IDA credit; and (ii) revision of the results framework to align it with the revised expectations
following the credit cancellation.

3.

Current Status of Project. The Project closed on March 31, 2020, with about 79 percent
of the revised loan amount disbursed.
4.

Under the Project, 1,077 water supply schemes were implemented. Most of these were
single-village schemes (SVSs) using local groundwater sources, and the remainder were larger
multi-village schemes (MVSs) that serve multiple communities with surface water from rivers. By
Project closing, 637 piped water schemes were formally commissioned across the four
participating states. The commissioned water schemes delivered water through 335,882 new,
metered, and piped household water connections, of which 41,809 had continuous 24/7 supply.
The Project also rehabilitated 20,879 piped household water connections and constructed or
rehabilitated 3,068 improved community water points. In the State of Jharkhand there are 189
schemes (182 SVSs and 7 MVSs).
5.

Overall, the Project supported rural water supply and sanitation programs in 33 districts in
Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand, and Uttar Pradesh, and directly benefitted about 3.97 million rural
people, including tribal populations. Forty-eight percent of the beneficiaries were female. About
2.31 million people were provided with access to “improved water sources” under the Project,
either through a new or rehabilitated piped household water connection, or improved community
water points. The Project also improved the “access and usage” of the water supply and sanitation
facilities created in the Project area. Women and children benefitted significantly from the Project
interventions as they bear a disproportionate burden of securing daily water supplies and dealing
with illnesses resulting from poor water and sanitation facilities.
6.

1
Official Use Only

 Summary of the Panel Process
7.
Request for Inspection. In 2018 the Inspection Panel (IPN or the Panel) registered two
requests relating to the Project. The First Request for Inspection of the Project, IPN Request
RQ18/06 was registered on November 5, 2018. The First Request included allegations by 104
Santhal tribal community members from the Giddhi Jhopri hamlet, who were affected by a Water
Treatment Plant (WTP) associated with the Bagbera MVS, which was supported under the Project.
On December 18, 2018, the Panel registered a Second Request on the Project (RQ18/07). The
Request raised allegations by 130 Santhal and Ho tribal community members from the Purani Basti
hamlet, who were affected by an Elevated Storage Reservoir (ESR), associated with the
Chhotagovindpur MVS, which was near their habitation. Both Giddhi Jhopri and Purani Basti are
small hamlets in the East Singhbum District of Jharkhand State; they are located on the outskirts
of the industrial city of Jamshedpur. Hereafter both the First Request and the Second Request will
be jointly referred to as “the Request,” and the Santhal community members from Giddhi Jhopri
and Purani Basti will be referred to as “the Requesters.”
8.
The Requesters argued that site selection did not adequately analyze alternatives that would
have avoided or minimized harm to their communities. They mainly complained that both the
WTP and ESR facilities were built on communal grounds of tribal or religious significance, which
in the case of Giddhi Jhopri also included their burial grounds. They alleged that this occurred
because appropriate consultations at the village level did not take place.

Management provided its Response to the two Requests on December 10, 2018 and
January 28, 2019. Because of the similarities in the cases and the close timing of the submissions,
the Panel decided to process the cases jointly. In its Eligibility Report to the Board on March 1,
2019, the Panel found the Request eligible for inspection and recommended that the Executive
Directors authorize an investigation.
9.

Investigation. The Board approved an investigation into the allegations of harm arising
from instances of noncompliance by the Bank with its operational policies and procedures. On
January 15, 2020, the Panel issued its Investigation Report to which Management responded on
December 21, 2022 with its proposed Management Action Plan (MAP). On March 2, 2023, the
Bank’s Board considered both reports and approved the MAP.
10.

II. PROGRESS OF MANAGEMENT ACTION PLAN IMPLEMENTATION

While most actions are completed, a few actions, particularly those linked to completion
and commissioning of the WTP at Bagbera, are still pending. Progress made in the current
reporting period and status of the MAP actions is as follows:
11.

o OP/BP 4.01 – Environmental Management Plans – Monthly Water Quality Testing:
Water quality testing, which was envisaged under both the Chhotagovindpur and Bagbera
schemes, has been completed for raw and treated water at Chhotagovindpur. The Drinking
Water and Sanitation Department (DWSD) will continue pre- and post-monsoon testing
there as part of its regular monitoring program. In the case of Bagbera, raw water testing
has been completed.
In terms of the status of construction of the WTP at Bagbera, the contractor has started
2
Official Use Only

 work on completion of the unfinished sections of the raw water pipe running from the
intake well to the WTP. Electromechanical dry testing of newly installed pumping
equipment at the intake well has been done and the equipment is now ready to operate as
soon as the remaining pipeline is laid. It is expected that the raw water rising main will be
completed by June 2026. The DWSD indicated that the Bagbera WTP is likely to be
commissioned at partial capacity, and water is expected to flow by June 2026. Once the
WTP at Bagbera is completed and commissioned, treated water quality testing will
commence as soon as operations begin and will be carried out monthly for a period of 12
months thereafter as planned. This action is completed for Chhotagovindpur and to be
completed for Bagbera.
o OP/BP 4.01 – Environmental Management Plans – Quarterly Progress Report on
Implementation of the Environmental Management Plan (EMP): The draft of the
consolidated Quarterly Progress Report on environmental monitoring for this fiscal year
was shared with the Bank, which reviewed it and found it to be satisfactory. This action is
completed for Chhotagovindpur and to be completed for Bagbera.
•

OP/BP 4.01 – Environmental Management Plans – Sludge Management: Sludge testing
for a period of 12 months was completed in the last reporting period for Chhotagovindpur.
Heavy metals were detected in the sludge but they were not sufficient to classify the sample
as hazardous. In the current reporting period, relevant measures for safe handling and
disposal have been put in place. Further, as requested and agreed with the DWSD, the Bank
team provided support in the preparation of Standard Operating Procedures for water
quality testing and sludge disposal. These Standard Operating Procedures have been shared
by the Executive Engineer DWSD with the WTP operator at Chhotagovindpur and will
also be utilized at Bagbera once the WTP is commissioned. For Bagbera, sludge testing
and subsequent review of sludge test reports remains pending as the WTP is still not
operational. The action will be initiated once operations start. In addition, the MAP action
pertaining to the review of information, education, and communication measures to be
taken up in case heavy metals are detected in the sludge for Bagbera remains pending until
the WTP is commissioned. This action is completed for Chhotagovindpur and to be
completed for Bagbera.

•

Solid and Liquid Waste Management (SLWM) Impacts – Liquid Waste Management:
During the current reporting period, no progress on SLWM coverage was made as no funds
were allocated this year by the Government of India for this central government scheme.
Once funds are allocated by the Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM), works will continue until
all Gram Panchayats in the state – including the Gram Panchayats of the Chhotagovindpur
and Bagbera schemes – are fully covered in due course. Given that LWM interventions
under SBM do not require separate Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) to be prepared, the
MAP action related to the Bank’s review of DPRs is no longer relevant. This
notwithstanding, the Bank reviewed the progress of LWM interventions shared in previous
Quarterly Progress Reports and followed up on the allocation of funds, which did not
materialize during the current reporting period. This action is ongoing.

•

Assessment of Impact on Indigenous Peoples – Consultation with Affected
Communities: As noted in the previous Progress Report, a Gram Sabha for the Bagbera
3

 scheme was held in Giddhi Jhopri, and the Bank reviewed the minutes and found them
satisfactory. The Bank will review the outcome of the Gram Sabha for Chhotagovindpur
once it is organized and monitor the implementation of agreed actions. This action is
completed for Bagbera and to be completed for Chhotagovindpur.

12.

1

•

Assessment of Impact on Indigenous Peoples – Livelihoods Pilot: The institutions (29
Self-Help Groups) that have been formed will continue. The funds provided from various
projects of the Government of Jharkhand and the central government will continue to be
rotated within the Self-Help Groups. All 29 1 Self-Help Groups have matured enough to be
able to apply for and receive loans from national banks for various livelihood /incomegenerating activities, such as small businesses, livestock raising, agriculture and vegetable
cultivation, as well as for other purposes such as health (treatment for ailments) and other
issues. As of this reporting period, the 29 Self-Help Groups have cumulatively received
INR 14.75 million. This action is completed.

•

Assessment of Impact on Indigenous Peoples – Slope Stabilization: Progress continues
to be made on slope stabilization works. Meetings have taken place between the Bank’s
technical expert, the DWSD, and its contracted consultant firm and the technical expert
provided recommendations on the design. This action is ongoing.

•

Consultations – Information Dissemination: The IEC District coordinator for the Jal
Jeevan Mission (JJM), with assistance from the JJM’s implementation support agency, is
conducting regular awareness and communication activities. This included a 15-day
intensive awareness program carried out between September 17, 2025 and October 2, 2025.
This action is completed.

•

Tribal development support to India portfolio: While the action related to Bank
supervision was completed as indicated in the first Progress Report, it is worth noting that
the Tribal Specialist (Consultant) already hired continues to provide support on Indigenous
Peoples Development Plans/Frameworks in Bank-financed operations in the India
portfolio.
Further details on progress in implementation of the MAP are provided in the table below.

Thirty Self-Help Groups were formed but two merged into one, reducing the total to 29.

 III. CONSULTATIONS WITH REQUESTERS ON THE MAP IMPLEMENTATION PROGRESS
13.
Stakeholder Consultations. On March 11, 2026, the Bank team met with the Requesters,
represented by Pargana Baba, the Requester from Giddhi Jhopri and two other representatives. The Bank
team apprised them of the following:
(i) Treated water quality testing had been completed for the Chhotagovindpur MVS, and no heavy
metals were found in the treated water originating from this scheme. However, the presence of
heavy metals was indicated in the sludge, albeit at concentration levels that are not hazardous. This
notwithstanding, the DWSD advised the WTP operator not to use the sludge for any edible crops
and to update its operating procedures for the WTP with this guidance.
(ii) Following the release of funds by the state government, works at the Bagbera WTP had resumed,
specifically on the intake well, pumps, and raw water rising mains. Work on the raw water rising
mains is expected to be completed within the next month. Water is expected to be supplied from at
least one clariflocculator at the WTP by June 30, 2026. Once the WTP is commissioned, sludge
testing will begin as well.
(iii) The designs and drawings for the slope stabilization at Bagbera were received with inputs from the
Bank consultant. Slope stabilization works will start once final comments from CDO are
incorporated and approval is obtained.
(iv) With respect to the livelihoods pilot, the 29 Self-Help Groups are functional and have received
loans for livelihood projects; it was also noted that through the Self-Help Groups, women from 300
households are being supported.
14.
The Requesters appreciated the update on the progress of the MAP actions and indicated the
following:
(i) They look forward to receiving treated drinking water in the coming summer and expressed the
desire to have such supply made available earlier than the stated target date of June 30, 2026, if
possible.
(ii) Given that slope stabilization works at Bagbera WTP will involve heavy machinery around the
boundary wall that might possibly impact the sacred tree, they requested to be informed before
commencement of works, so that they could organize a Gram Sabha to inform everyone about the
activity before the works start.

IV. NEXT STEPS
15.

16.
Next Progress Report. The next Progress Report will be provided to the Board in 12 months’ time,
or upon completion of the MAP, whichever occurs first.

abstract: This is the Third Progress Report to the Board of Executive Directors (the Board) on the implementation of the Management Action Plan (MAP) in response to the Inspection Panel Investigation Report on the India - Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Project for Low Income States. The Project was a US$1.0 billion operation, of which the International Development Association (IDA) financed US$500 million equivalent, and the rest was funded by the Government of India (34 percent), the governments of the Project states (16 percent) and beneficiary contributions (0.1 percent). The Project was approved on December 30, 2013, with a planned duration of six years. Implemented in the states of Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh, the Project supported investments to improve water supply and sanitation, including construction of new infrastructure and rehabilitation and expansion of existing schemes. The Project was restructured in 2019. This included: (i) cancellation of US$250 million of the IDA credit; and (ii) revision of the results framework to align it with the revised expectations following the credit cancellation.
